note.explanation: Carbohydrates are grouped by how many sugar units they contain. Monosaccharides have one unit, disaccharides have two, and polysaccharides have hundreds to thousands. Their taste and solubility also differ.
examples: Glucose is a monosaccharide; sucrose is a disaccharide.
Starch is a polysaccharide found in plants.
note.checkAnswer: Monosaccharides are single sugar molecules; disaccharides contain two monosaccharide units; polysaccharides contain hundreds to thousands of monosaccharide units.
note.simple: Think of sugar units like building blocks: one block is a monosaccharide, two joined blocks are a disaccharide, and a very long chain is a polysaccharide.
note.checkQuestion: How many monosaccharide units make up a disaccharide?
note.title: The three classes of carbohydrates
steps: Look for how many sugar units the carbohydrate contains.
One unit means monosaccharide; two units mean disaccharide; a very large number means polysaccharide.
Use taste and solubility as extra clues: monosaccharides are sweet and easily soluble, disaccharides are less sweet and less soluble, and polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble.
note.answer: A disaccharide is made of two monosaccharide units.

modelAnswer: Monosaccharides are simple sugars made of a single sugar molecule.
They are easily soluble in water and have a sweet taste; glucose, fructose, and galactose are examples of hexoses.
Disaccharides are made of two monosaccharide units and are less soluble in water and less sweet.
Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose, while maltose is made of two glucose molecules.
Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharide units; they are insoluble in water and tasteless.
Starch is a plant storage polysaccharide, glycogen is animal starch stored mainly in liver and muscles, and cellulose is found in plant cell walls.
Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy; dietary fibre helps proper bowel movements, and cellulose supports plant cells.

Answer: The three classes are monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides; they contain one, two, and many monosaccharide units respectively and have important energy, fibre, storage, transport, and structural roles.

explain.title: Carbohydrates and their classes
explain.body: “Carbohydrate” means ‘hydrated carbons’. They are the organic compounds in which the ratio of H and O is 2:1 (same as in water). They are also known as “Saccharides” (meaning sugar). They have the general formula Cₙ(H₂O)ₙ where n is the number of carbon atoms. There are three classes of carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides.

explain.title: Monosaccharides
explain.body: Monosaccharides (simple sugars) are made of single sugar molecule. They are easily soluble in water and have sweet taste. They may have 3 to 7 carbon atoms. Pentoses (5 C) and hexoses (6 C) are most common. Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses; glucose, fructose, and galactose are hexoses.

explain.title: Disaccharides and polysaccharides
explain.body: Disaccharides are made of two monosaccharides units. They are less soluble in water and are less sweet in taste. Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose; maltose is made of two glucose molecules. Polysaccharides are large molecules composed of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides units. They are insoluble in water and are tasteless. Examples include starch, glycogen, cellulose, and chitin.

explain.title: Sources and functions
explain.body: Carbohydrates are the primary source of energy. Glucose is used by cells to produce energy through cellular respiration. Dietary fibre contains indigestible carbohydrates e.g., cellulose. It helps for the proper bowel movements. Ribose and deoxyribose are essential parts of RNA and DNA respectively. Plants convert monosaccharides to disaccharides like sucrose for transport. Cellulose supports plant cells and ultimately the whole plant.

mistakes: Do not confuse sucrose with maltose: sucrose is glucose plus fructose, while maltose is two glucose molecules.
Do not call starch a disaccharide; it is a polysaccharide.
Do not say all carbohydrates are sweet or soluble: polysaccharides are tasteless and insoluble in water.
When giving a role for cellulose, distinguish its structural support in plants from its role as dietary fibre in bowel movements.
Do not mix up plant starch and animal glycogen: starch is stored in plants, while glycogen is mainly stored in the liver and muscles.
